Abnormalities of Placental Implantation
Several types of abnormal placental implantations are associated with significant complications.

Placenta previa is a condition in which the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment completely or partially covering the cervix, which can lead to serious third trimester bleeding. A complete placenta previa requires cesarean delivery to avert placental rupture and fatal maternal and fetal **hemorrhage** during vaginal delivery.

Placenta accreta spectrum disorder is caused by complete absence of the decidua (at least focally), such that the placental villous tissue is in direct contact with the myometrium (Fig. 22.49) and hence invades, or penetrates completely through the myometrium, sometimes CHAPTER ₂₂ The Female Genital Tract 937 even adhering to serosal surfaces or pelvic organs. It leads to a failure of placental separation at birth and is an important cause of severe, potentially life-threatening postpartum bleeding. Common predisposing factors are placenta previa (in up to 60% of cases) and previous cesarean delivery or other uterine surgery that breached the endometrial lining and caused scarring.
Placental Infections

Infections in the placenta develop by two pathways: (1) ascending infection through the birth canal and (2) hematogenous (transplacental) infection due to maternal **sepsis**, viremia, or parasitemia. Ascending infections are by far the most common and are virtually always bacterial; in many such instances, localized infection of the membranes produces premature rupture of membranes and preterm delivery. The amniotic fluid may be cloudy with purulent **exudate**, and histologically the chorion-amnion contains an infiltrate of maternal neutrophils (maternal inflammatory response) (Fig. 22.50A–B). The infection frequently elicits a fetal response consisting of a “**vasculitis**” of the umbilical vessels and/or fetal chorionic plate vessels (fetal inflammatory response). Of note, intense fetal inflammatory responses are associated with perinatal morbidity and an increased risk for the development of cerebral palsy.
Uncommonly, bacterial infections can result from hematogenous spread to the placenta, leading to acute villitis (Fig. 22.50C).

Several microbes of the TORCH group (toxoplasmosa and others [**syphilis**, tuberculosis, listeriosis], rubella, cytomegalovirus (Fig. 22.50D), herpes simplex), can infect the placenta via the hematogenous route. They typically give rise to chronic inflammatory cell infiltrates in the chorionic villi (chronic villitis) and are associated with fetal growth restriction (Chapter 10).
Preeclampsia and Eclampsia

Preeclampsia is a systemic syndrome characterized by widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction that presents after 20 weeks of gestation with new onset hypertension and at least one of other findings, such as edema and proteinuria. Preeclampsia and eclampsia account for.50,000 maternal deaths yearly worldwide. Preeclampsia is most prevalent among Black and Hispanic patients, resulting in approximately 26% of maternal deaths among this population in the United States. It occurs in about 3% to 5% of pregnant females, usually in the last trimester and more commonly in females pregnant for the first time (primiparas). Some of these females become seriously ill, developing seizures; this particularly severe form of the disorder is termed eclampsia. Other complications stemming from systemic endothelial dysfunction include hypercoagulability, acute renal failure, and pulmonary edema. Approximately 10% of females with preeclampsia develop microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, referred to as the HELLP syndrome (Chapter 14). Preeclampsia should be distinguished from gestational hypertension that can develop in pregnancy without the other symptoms/signs of preeclampsia.
Pathogenesis

The placenta plays a central role in the pathogenesis of preeclampsia, as symptoms almost always disappear rapidly after its delivery. The critical abnormalities in preeclampsia are diffuse endothelial dysfunction, vasoconstriction (leading to hypertension), and increased vascular permeability (resulting in proteinuria and edema). These effects are most likely mediated by placenta-derived factor(s) released into the maternal circulation. Although the release of these factors and the clinical syndrome develop late in gestation, the pathogenesis of the disease appears to be closely tied to the earliest events of pregnancy and placentation. The principal pathophysiologic aberrations are proposed to be:

Failure of the normal physiologic remodeling of the placental bed vessels. The precipitating events in **preeclampsia** are abnormally shallow trophoblastic implantation and a failure of physiologic remodeling of the maternal vessels, which is required for adequate perfusion of the placenta. At the implantation site of a normal pregnancy, fetal extravillous trophoblast invade the maternal decidua and decidual vessels, destroy the vascular smooth muscle, and replace the maternal endothelial cells with fetal trophoblastic cells, forming hybrid fetomaternal blood vessels. This process converts the decidual spiral arteries from small-caliber resistance vessels to large-capacity low-resistance uteroplacental vessels lacking a smooth muscle coat (Fig. 22.51). In preeclampsia, this vascular remodeling fails to occur, leaving the placenta ill equipped to meet the increased circulatory demands of late gestation and setting the stage for the development of placental **ischemia**.

Endothelial dysfunction and imbalance of angiogenic and antiangiogenic factors. It is postulated that in response to **hypoxia**, the ischemic placenta releases factors into the maternal circulation that cause an imbalance in circulating angiogenic and anti-angiogenic factors; this, in turn, leads to systemic maternal endothelial dysfunction and the clinical manifestations of the disease. In support of this, the blood levels of two placenta-derived antiangiogenic factors, soluble feline McDonough sarcoma (FMS)-like tyrosine kinase (sFLT-1) and endoglin, which antagonize the effects of VEGF and TGFb, respectively, are several orders of magnitude higher in females with preeclampsia than in healthy controls. In preeclampsia, high levels of sFlt1 and soluble endoglin bring about a decrease in **angiogenesis** much earlier than in normal pregnancy, resulting in defective placental vascular development. Furthermore, TGFb induces endothelial production of nitric oxide, a potent vasodilator; thus, inhibition of TGFb by endoglin may directly contribute to systemic vasoconstriction, hypertension, and tissue hypoperfusion. Studies in animal models also implicate sFlt l and soluble endoglin in the pathogenesis of endothelial dysfunction.

When sFLT1 and endoglin are overexpressed together, pregnant rats develop nephrotic-range proteinuria, severe hypertension, as well as features of the HELLP syndrome, including elevated liver enzymes, decreased platelet count, and hemolysis, while their pups are growth restricted, all hallmarks of severe preeclampsia. Thus, it seems that sFlt1 and soluble endoglin are key mediators that link the placenta to the characteristic maternal endothelial dysfunction of preeclampsia.

MORPHOLOGY

The placenta reveals several microscopic changes of maternal vascular malperfusion. These include (1) placental **hypoplasia**, (2) placental infarcts, which can be large and numerous, (3) exaggerated ischemic changes in the chorionic villi and trophoblast, consisting of increased syncytial knots and small shrunken villi with increased maternal vascular space (distal villous hypoplasia), (4) frequent retroplacental **hematomas** due to bleeding and instability of uteroplacental vessels, and (5) abnormal decidual vessels, which may show thrombi, lack of normal remodeling (described earlier), **fibrinoid necrosis**, or intimal lipid deposition (acute atherosis) (Fig. 22.52). When present, liver lesions take the form of irregular, focal, subcapsular, and intraparenchymal **hemorrhages**. On histologic examination, there are fibrin thrombi in the portal capillaries and foci of hemorrhagic necrosis.

Clinical Features

Preeclampsia/eclampsia is an important cause of maternal and fetal mortality worldwide due to hypertensive crises, strokes, and abnormal bleeding due to disseminated intravascular coagulation. Preeclampsia most commonly occurs after 34 weeks of gestation but begins earlier in females with hydatidiform mole (discussed later) or preexisting kidney disease, hypertension, or coagulopathies. The onset is typically marked by hypertension and edema, with proteinuria appearing several days later. Headaches and visual disturbances may follow and are indicative of preeclampsia with severe features, often requiring early delivery. Eclampsia is heralded by more severe central nervous system involvement, including seizures, eventual coma, and even death. Management of preeclampsia differs depending on the gestational age and severity of disease. For term pregnancies, delivery is the treatment of choice regardless of disease severity. For preterm pregnancies in which delivery place the fetus at risk, mild disease can be managed ex-pectantly by controlling maternal hypertension and by close monitoring of the mother and fetus. However, eclampsia, preeclampsia with severe features, fetal compromise, or the HELLP syndrome are indications for delivery regardless of gestational age.

Following delivery, proteinuria and hypertension usually disappear within 1 to 2 weeks later. Although in most instances preeclampsia has no lasting sequelae, about 20% of affected females develop hypertension and microalbuminuria within 7 years of a pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia. There is also a two-fold increase in the long-term risk of cardiovascular disease.

Hydatidiform Mole

**Hydatidiform moles** are important to recognize because they are associated with an increased risk of persistent trophoblastic disease (invasive mole) or **choriocarcinoma**. Moles are characterized histologically by cystic swelling of the chorionic villi and circumferential biphasic trophoblastic **hyperplasia**. They are usually diagnosed during early pregnancy (average 9 weeks) by pelvic sonography. Molar pregnancy can develop at any age, but the risk is higher at the two ends of reproductive life, during puberty and in perimenopausal females. For unknown reasons, the incidence varies considerably in different parts of the world. Hydatidiform mole occurs in about 1 in 1000 to 2000 pregnancies in the United States, but it is twice as common in Southeast Asia. Two types of noninvasive moles—complete and partial—can be identified by cytogenetic and histologic studies.
Complete Mole

Complete mole results from fertilization of an egg that has lost (or subsequently loses) its female chromosomes, and as a result its nuclear genetic material is completely paternally derived. Ninety percent have a diploid 46,XX karyotype stemming from duplication of the genetic material of one sperm (a phenomenon called androgenesis that produces monospermic complete hydatidiform mole) (Fig. 22.53A). The remaining 10% result from the fertilization of an “empty” egg by two sperm (dispermic complete hydatidiform mole) (Fig. 22.53B); these may have a 46,XX or 46,XY karyotype. In complete moles, there is no embryonic development. Patients have 2.5% risk of subsequent choriocarcinoma and a 15% risk of persistent or invasive mole.
Partial Mole

Partial moles result from fertilization of an egg with two sperm (Fig. 22.53C). In these moles, the karyotype is triploid (e.g., 69,XXY) or occasionally tetraploid (92,XXXY). Fetal development may be seen, but the fetus is characteristically growth restricted and has lethal anomalies of the central nervous system as well as skeletal abnormalities such as syndactyly. Partial moles have an increased risk of persistent molar disease but are not typically associated with postmolar choriocarcinoma.
MORPHOLOGY

Grossly, classic hydatidiform moles appear as a delicate, friable mass of thin-walled, translucent, cystic, grapelike structures consisting of swollen edematous (hydropic) villi (Fig. 22.54A). In complete mole, the microscopic abnormalities involve all or most of the villous tissue. The chorionic villi are enlarged, smooth and oval with central cavitation (cisterns) and are covered by a trophoblast proliferation that includes both cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts (Fig. 22.54B). In contrast, in partial moles, only a fraction of the villi is enlarged and edematous, the trophoblastic hyperplasia is focal and less marked, and only syncytiotrophoblasts are hyperplastic. Partial moles have irregular villous outlines, unlike the smooth round outlines of a complete mole, often with prominent trophoblastic inclusions (Fig. 22.55).

Invasive Mole

Invasive mole is an infiltrative lesion that penetrates and sometimes perforates the uterine wall. Invasive moles manifest clinically with vaginal bleeding, irregular uterine enlargement, and persistently elevated serum HCG. Bleeding is due to invasion of the myometrium by hydropic chorionic villi lined by proliferating cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast. The principal therapy is surgical evacuation of the uterus or hysterectomy. In some instances, however, the villi invade parametrial tissue and blood vessels and embolize to distant sites, such as the lungs and brain. Lung metastases occur in about 5% of complete hydatidiform moles. Small (,2cm) lung metastases usually spontaneously regress and do not require chemotherapy. By contrast, larger metastases require treatment to prevent progressive disease.
Choriocarcinoma

Gestational choriocarcinoma is a malignant neoplasm of trophoblastic cells originating from a previously normal or abnormal pregnancy, such as an extrauterine **ectopic pregnancy** or a complete hydatidiform mole. Gestational choriocarcinoma is an uncommon condition that arises in 1 in 20,000 to 30,000 pregnancies in the United States. It may be preceded by several conditions; 50% arise after a complete hydatidiform mole, 25% follow spontaneous abortions, approximately 22% follow normal pregnancies, and the remainder occurr after ectopic pregnancies or arise in the placenta during pregnancy. Choriocarcinoma is characterized by destructive and hemorrhagic invasion and is often widely metastatic at presentation. Once identified, it responds well to chemotherapy and is considered a curable disease. Rarely, nongestational choriocarcinoma develops from germ cells in the ovaries or the mediastinum. These tumors are morphologically identical to gestational choriocarcinoma but can be distinguished by the absence of paternally derived DNA, which is present in all gestational choriocarcinomas. Nongestational choriocarcinomas do not have as good a prognosis as gestational choriocarcinomas.

MORPHOLOGY

**Choriocarcinoma** is a soft, fleshy, yellow-white tumor that usually has large pale areas of necrosis and extensive **hemorrhage** (Fig. 22.56A). Histologically, it consists of proliferating syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts (Fig. 22.56B); chorionic villi are absent. Mitoses are abundant and sometimes abnormal. The tumor invades the underlying myometrium, frequently penetrates blood vessels, and in some cases extends to the uterine serosa and adjacent structures.
Clinical Features

Gestational choriocarcinoma usually manifests as irregular vaginal spotting of a bloody, brown fluid. This discharge may appear during an apparently normal pregnancy, after a miscarriage, or after curettage. Sometimes the tumor does not appear until months after these events. This tumor has high propensity for hematogenous spread and by the time it is discovered imaging of the chest and bones may disclose the presence of metastatic lesions. The HCG levels are typically elevated to levels above those encountered in **hydatidiform moles**, but occasional tumors produce little hormone and some tumors are so necrotic that HCG levels are low. Widespread metastases are characteristic; the most common sites are the lungs (50%) and vagina (30% to 40%), followed by, in descending order of frequency, the brain, liver, bone, and kidney.

Intraplacental choriocarcinoma can present as a grossly identifiable mass or with widespread **metastasis**. It seems likely that all postgesta-tional choriocarcinomas originate within the placenta but are not recognized at delivery, possibly due to small size. For this reason, all placental masses must be carefully examined histologically.

Treatment of gestational choriocarcinoma depends on the stage of the tumor and usually consists of evacuation of the uterine contents and chemotherapy. Chemotherapy is highly effective, with nearly 100% remission rate and high rates of cure. Many cured patients have normal subsequent pregnancies and deliveries. By contrast, rare nongestational choriocarcinomas arising outside of the uterus are more difficult to treat.
